text:
CHRISTIAN:
  What did you say?

ROXANE:
  So much the worse for you if I run these risks!
  It is your letters that have intoxicated me! Ah! just think
  How many you have written me over the past month,
  And always more beautiful!

CHRISTIAN:
  What! For a few little
  Love letters...

ROXANE:
  Be quiet! You cannot know!
  My God, I adored you, it is true, ever since one evening,
  In a voice I had not known you possessed, beneath my window,
  Your soul began to make itself known...
  Well! Your letters, you see, for the past month,
  Have been as though all the while I were hearing it, your voice
  From that evening, so tender, and which enfolds you!
  So much the worse for you, I hasten here. The wise Penelope
  Would not have remained beneath her roof embroidering,
  Had Lord Ulysses written like you;
  But to join him, as mad as Helen,
  She too would have sent her balls of wool packing!...

CHRISTIAN:
  But...

ROXANE:
  I read, I reread, I swooned,
  I was yours. Each of those little sheets
  Was like a petal blown from your soul.
  In every word of those letters of flame one feels
  Powerful, sincere love...

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah! Sincere and powerful?
  One can feel that, Roxane?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! One certainly can!

CHRISTIAN:
  And you have come?...

ROXANE:
  I have come (oh, my Christian, my master!
  You would raise me up if I wished to kneel
  At your feet, so it is my soul that I lay there,
  And you will never be able to raise it again!)
  I have come to ask your forgiveness (and it is indeed the hour
  To ask forgiveness, since we may die!)
  For having at first, in my frivolity,
  Insulted you by loving you for your beauty alone!

CHRISTIAN (in terror):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  And later, my friend, less frivolous,
  —A bird that hops before it fully takes flight—
  Your beauty holding me back, your soul drawing me onward,
  I loved you for both together!...

CHRISTIAN:
  And now?

ROXANE:
  Well! At last, you yourself have triumphed over yourself,
  And now it is only for your soul that I love you!

CHRISTIAN (recoiling):
  Ah! Roxane!

ROXANE:
  Then be happy. For to be loved
  Only for that in which one is costumed for a moment
  Must torture an eager and noble heart;
  But your dear mind effaces your face,
  And the beauty through which you pleased me at first,
  Now I see more clearly... and I no longer see it!

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh!...

ROXANE:
  Do you still doubt such a victory?...

CHRISTIAN (painfully):
  Roxane!

ROXANE:
  I understand, you cannot believe
  In this love?...

CHRISTIAN:
  I do not want this love!
  I want to be loved more simply for...

ROXANE:
  For
  What women have loved in you until now?
  Then let yourself be loved in a better way!

CHRISTIAN:
  No! It was better before!

ROXANE:
  Ah! You understand nothing about it!
  It is now that I love better, that I love truly!
  It is what makes you yourself, do you hear me, that I adore!
  And less brilliant...

CHRISTIAN:
  Be quiet!

ROXANE:
  I would love you still!
  If all your beauty suddenly flew away...

CHRISTIAN:
  Oh! Do not say that!

ROXANE:
  Yes, I do say it!

CHRISTIAN:
  What? Ugly?

ROXANE:
  Ugly! I swear it!

CHRISTIAN:
  God!

ROXANE:
  And is your joy profound?

CHRISTIAN (in a stifled voice):
  Yes...

ROXANE:
  What is the matter with you?

CHRISTIAN (gently pushing her away):
  Nothing. Two words to say: one second...

ROXANE:
  But?...

CHRISTIAN (showing her a group of cadets at the back):
  My love took you away from those poor fellows:
  Go and smile upon them a little, since they are going to die... go!

ROXANE (moved):
  Dear Christian!...
  (She goes upstage toward the Gascons, who respectfully crowd around
  her.)



Scene 4.IX.

Christian, Cyrano; at the back, Roxane conversing with Carbon and several cadets.


CHRISTIAN (calling toward Cyrano's tent):
  Cyrano?

CYRANO (reappearing, armed for battle):
  What is it? You are deathly pale!

CHRISTIAN:
  She no longer loves me!

CYRANO:
  What?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is you she loves!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  She loves only my soul now!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes!
  So it is indeed you she loves—and you love her too!

CYRANO:
  I?

CHRISTIAN:
  I know it.

CYRANO:
  It is true.

CHRISTIAN:
  Like a madman.

CYRANO:
  More than that.

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her!

CYRANO:
  No!

CHRISTIAN:
  Why?

CYRANO:
  Look at my face!

CHRISTIAN:
  She would love me ugly!

CYRANO:
  She told you that!

CHRISTIAN:
  Just now!

CYRANO:
  Ah! I am very glad she told you that!
  But come, come, do not believe such a mad thing!
  —My God, I am glad she thought
  To say it—but come, do not take her at her word;
  Come, do not become ugly: she would hold it against me too much!

CHRISTIAN:
  That is what I want to see!

CYRANO:
  No, no!

CHRISTIAN:
  Let her choose!
  You are going to tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  No, no! Not that torture.

CHRISTIAN:
  Should I destroy your happiness because I am handsome?
  It is too unjust!

CYRANO:
  And should I send yours to the grave
  Because, thanks to the accident of birth,
  I have the gift of expressing... what you perhaps feel?

CHRISTIAN:
  Tell her everything!

CYRANO:
  He persists in tempting me; it is wrong!

CHRISTIAN:
  I am weary of carrying a rival within myself!

CYRANO:
  Christian!

CHRISTIAN:
  Our union—without witnesses—clandestine,
  —Can be broken—if we survive!

CYRANO:
  He persists!...

CHRISTIAN:
  Yes, I want to be loved for myself, or not at all!
  —I am going to see what they are doing, there! I will go to the far end
  Of the outpost; I will return: speak, and let her prefer
  One of the two of us!

CYRANO:
  It will be you!

CHRISTIAN:
  But... I hope so!
  (He calls):
  Roxane!

CYRANO:
  No! No!

ROXANE (running over):
  What is it?

CHRISTIAN:
  Cyrano will tell you
  Something important...
  (She goes quickly to Cyrano. Christian exits.)



Scene 4.X.

Roxane, Cyrano, then Le Bret, Carbon de Castel-Jaloux, the cadets,
Ragueneau, de Guiche, etc.


ROXANE:
  Important?
